content: The anemia associated with chronic kidney disease (CKD) can be worsened by iron deficiency. Iron supplementation can be administered either intravenously (IV) or orally, and each route has its own advantages and disadvantages. However, it remains uncertain whether the potential risks and additional costs of IV iron are justified compared to oral iron. This review aimed to evaluate the benefits and harms of IV iron supplementation compared to oral iron in adults and children with CKD, including those on dialysis, those with kidney transplants, and those with CKD not requiring dialysis. The review included 39 studies involving 3,852 participants, with 11 studies added in this update. A low risk of bias was identified in 51% of studies for sequence generation, 36% for allocation concealment, 56% for attrition bias, and 51% for selective outcome reporting. However, all studies were at high risk of performance bias due to the lack of blinding. Despite this, detection bias was considered low because the primary outcomes were laboratory-based and unlikely to be influenced by the lack of blinding. There is insufficient evidence to suggest that IV iron, compared to oral iron, has any significant effect on all-cause mortality (11 studies, 1,952 participants: risk ratio [RR] 1.12, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.64 to 1.94), the need to initiate dialysis (4 studies, 743 participants: RR 0.81, 95% CI 0.41 to 1.61), or the need for blood transfusions (5 studies, 774 participants: RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.34). These analyses were assessed as having low-certainty evidence. It is also uncertain whether IV iron reduces cardiovascular mortality, as the evidence for this outcome was of very low certainty (3 studies, 206 participants: RR 1.71, 95% CI 0.41 to 7.18). Quality of life was assessed in five studies, with four reporting no difference between IV and oral iron, and one study reporting an improvement in participants treated with IV iron. IV iron may increase the risk of allergic reactions or hypotension (15 studies, 2,607 participants: RR 3.56, 95% CI 1.88 to 6.74), with an absolute harm of 24 per 1,000 participants with IV iron compared to 7 per 1,000 with oral iron. However, IV iron may reduce the risk of gastrointestinal adverse effects (14 studies, 1,986 participants: RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.33 to 0.66), with an absolute benefit of 150 per 1,000 participants with IV iron compared to 319 per 1,000 with oral iron. These analyses were also assessed as having low-certainty evidence. IV iron may increase the number of participants achieving target hemoglobin levels (13 studies, 2,206 participants: RR 1.71, 95% CI 1.43 to 2.04), with an absolute benefit of 542 per 1,000 participants with IV iron compared to 317 per 1,000 with oral iron. It may also increase hemoglobin levels (31 studies, 3,373 participants: mean difference [MD] 0.72 g/dL, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.05), ferritin levels (33 studies, 3,389 participants: MD 224.84 µg/L, 95% CI 165.85 to 283.83), and transferrin saturation (27 studies, 3,089 participants: MD 7.69%, 95% CI 5.10 to 10.28). Additionally, IV iron may reduce the required dose of erythropoietin-stimulating agents (ESAs) (11 studies, 522 participants: standardized mean difference [SMD] -0.72, 95% CI -1.12 to -0.31) while having little or no effect on glomerular filtration rate (8 studies, 1,052 participants: MD 0.83 mL/min, 95% CI -0.79 to 2.44). These analyses were assessed as having low-certainty evidence, and there was moderate to high heterogeneity in the results. Meta-regression did not identify clear reasons for this heterogeneity. In conclusion, the evidence suggests that IV iron may increase hemoglobin, ferritin, and transferrin saturation levels in CKD patients, as well as the number of participants achieving target hemoglobin levels, while reducing ESA requirements. However, there is insufficient evidence to determine whether IV iron has any effect on all-cause mortality, cardiovascular mortality, or quality of life. Adverse effects were reported in only half of the included studies, and IV iron was associated with a higher risk of allergic reactions or hypotension but a lower risk of gastrointestinal side effects. Further studies focusing on patient-centered outcomes, longer follow-up periods, and the cost-effectiveness of IV iron are needed to determine whether its use is justified.
